intro: Nine of these eleven trees stand within a kilometre of Cathedral Square, five of them in Bernardinų sodas and four in the courtyards of the old university, which makes most of the list one afternoon on foot. The garden's speciality is trunks in multiples: a willow with nine, a lime with four, an ash whose sources cannot agree on three or four. A protected pine adds 1.3 km up the Song Valley slope. The city's oldest lime, its top broken off by a storm in 2023, stands alone in Antakalnis, 2.2 km out and a stop of its own.
meta_description: Eleven remarkable trees in Vilnius, nine within one kilometre: a nine-trunked willow, a shrine carved into a lime, and an oak of over 400 years.
question_meta: Vilnius's oldest tree is an oak in Bernardinai Garden, over 400 years old and five metres round. Where it stands, and ten more across the city.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Vilnius is an oak in Bernardinai Garden, at the southern end of the park near the footbridge over the Vilnia, about ten minutes on foot from Cathedral Square. It is put at over four hundred years old, measures roughly five metres round, and the municipal register gives it no name beyond Seniausias azuolas, the oldest oak. It has been protected as a heritage object since 29 May 1996. Its recent history is more dramatic than its age. Construction and transformer works beside it destroyed an estimated eighty percent of its root system, damage that only became clear when the garden was overhauled in 2012. Arborists took some twenty tonnes of weight out of the crown so the roots still working could carry what was left, then cleaned and sealed the cavities in the trunk. It survived, and the city still points visitors towards it. One caution about the number: none of the sources that give the four hundred years says how it was arrived at, so read it as the received figure rather than a ring count. Four more protected trees stand within a few hundred metres, which makes this a stop on a walk rather than a destination on its own. The city's oldest lime is a separate tree, put at 300 to 350 years and standing 2.2 km away in Antakalnis, and a storm took its top off in 2023.
question_context: Lithuania's state register of protected natural objects records this tree's position and its designation date and very little else: it has no age field, no girth field and no height field. That is why eight of the eleven trees on the Vilnius page carry no age at all, and why the pages say so plainly instead of offering a guess. The figures here come from the register for position and designation, and from Lithuanian encyclopedia and Wikipedia entries for the rest. Several of those state their own coordinates independently and land within ten metres of the register's, which is what puts most of these pins at confirmed. Two are approximate, the pine in Kalnų parkas and the cork trees in Bernardinų sodas, because the register rounds their coordinates and nothing sharper exists. Where two sources disagree, the tree's own page says so rather than picking a winner: the multi-stemmed ash in Bernardinų sodas is listed with three trunks by the register and four by the garden's own inventory, and both counts are on its page. A reader who counts when they get there settles it faster than desk research can. See the full list of eleven on the Vilnius page.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Vilnius?
faq.a: An oak in Bernardinai Garden, put at over four hundred years old and roughly five metres round, protected since 1996 and listed with no name beyond the oldest oak. It lost about eighty percent of its root system to nearby construction, and in 2012 arborists removed roughly twenty tonnes from the crown to save it.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Nine of the eleven, yes. Five stand in Bernardinai Garden, which is also called Sereikiškių Park, and four more in the courtyards of Vilnius University's central buildings a few minutes away; that loop runs about a kilometre from Cathedral Square. The pine in Kalnų parkas adds 1.3 km up the Song Valley slope. The eleventh, the city's oldest lime, stands 2.2 km out in Antakalnis and is a separate trip.

Yes, all eleven. Bernardinai Garden is a public park open daily, Kalnų parkas is open at all hours, Sapiegos parkas in Antakalnis is a public park, and the university courtyards are open to the public during the day.

faq.q: Why do so many of them have no age?
faq.a: Because nobody has measured them. Lithuania's register of protected trees carries no age, girth or height field, and for eight of these eleven no published source gives a figure either. Rather than guess, the pages say so and ask readers who have looked, or measured, to tell us.

trees.name: The Oldest Oak of Vilnius

location.address: Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiškių Park), southern edge near the entrance from Šv. Brunono Bonifaco street, close to the pedestrian bridge over the Vilnia

trees.story:
This oak lost roughly eighty percent of its root system and is still alive. The damage was done slowly and out of sight, by construction and transformer works beside it, and only became clear when Bernardinai Garden was overhauled in 2012. The rescue was blunt. Arborists took some twenty tonnes of weight out of the crown so the roots still working could carry what was left, then cleaned and treated the cavities in the trunk. Fourteen years later it is still the tree the city points people towards.

Its official entry does not bother with a name. It is listed simply as Seniausias ąžuolas, the oldest oak, protected as a municipal heritage object since 29 May 1996, with a trunk about five metres round. The sources put it at over four hundred years and none of them says how that figure was arrived at, so read it as the received number rather than a measurement.

It stands at the southern end of the garden, close to the footbridge over the Vilnia, which puts it a few minutes from Cathedral Square and a few steps from Užupis. Three more protected trees stand within a few hundred metres of it, so this is a stop on a walk rather than a destination on its own.
trees.access: Free, inside Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiškių Park), open daily
trees.transport: Short walk (10-15 min) from Cathedral Square / Vilnius Old Town centre
trees.how_to_recognise: One heavy trunk about five metres round, at the southern end of the garden near the footbridge over the Vilnia. The crown looks short for the girth because roughly twenty tonnes were taken out of it in 2012.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Daukantas Memorial Oak

location.address: S. Daukantas Courtyard, Vilnius University central buildings, Old Town

trees.story:
The tree commemorates a walk. Simonas Daukantas, the 19th-century historian, came to Vilnius University on foot from Žemaitija, and the oak that carries his name in the courtyard named after him was grown from an acorn brought back from that same corner of the country.

It is not an old tree, and it is not here for that. Nobody has published a planting date. Lithuanian Wikipedia says it went in for the university's 400th anniversary, and since the university was founded in 1579 that points at 1979 and an age of about forty-seven. The year is arithmetic on the anniversary, not something any source states.

The planting did not go smoothly either. Two earlier saplings failed and were replaced, and some of those survivors are now said to stand next door in the Sirvydas Courtyard, which is why accounts of which oak is which do not entirely line up. The tree Vilnius protects under this name, listed as a heritage object since 29 May 1996, is the one at this pin.

Daukantas walked from Žemaitija to study here, which in the 1810s was a serious undertaking rather than a gesture. The tree is the university's way of keeping the walk in the ground. If you know which oak is which, or when this one actually went in, tell us.
trees.access: Free, inside a Vilnius University courtyard open to the public during the day
trees.transport: Short walk (5-10 min) from Cathedral Square
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak in the Daukantas courtyard itself. Some accounts place replacement saplings from the same planting next door in the Sirvydas courtyard, so the two get confused; this pin is the tree the city protects under this name.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Linden of Daukša Courtyard

location.address: M. Daukšos Courtyard, Universiteto g. 7, Vilnius University central buildings

trees.story:
Somebody has carved a chapel into this tree. It is a small niche cut into the trunk with a two-pitched roof above it, and inside stands a wooden figure of an old warrior holding a sword. No source names the carver. Lithuania has a long tradition of little roofed wooden shrines by roads and in yards, but putting one inside a living lime in a university courtyard is not the usual practice.

The tree holds the M. Daukša Courtyard of Vilnius University's central buildings together. History Faculty students meet under it, alumni come back to it at reunions, and the student corporation Korp! Tilia is said to have taken its name from it. Tilia is the linden's own genus, which makes the name either a good joke or a flat description.

Vilnius has protected it as a municipal heritage object since 29 May 1996. What nobody has written down is how old it is. There is no year in the register, none in the literature, and no published girth to reason back from. If you have measured it, or know when it went in, tell us and it goes on the page.
trees.access: Free, inside a Vilnius University courtyard open to the public during the day
trees.transport: Short walk (5-10 min) from Cathedral Square
trees.how_to_recognise: Unmistakable once you are close: a small roofed shrine is carved into the trunk, with a wooden warrior figure inside it.

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.name: The Ash of Mickiewicz's Courtyard

location.address: Adomas Mickevičius Courtyard, Vilnius University central buildings

trees.story:
Vilnius has protected this ash since 1996 and nobody has recorded a single measurement of it. No height, no girth, no age. The register gives the name and the coordinates and stops there, which is unusual for a tree a city considers worth protecting.

It stands in the Adomas Mickevičius Courtyard of the university's central buildings, named for the Romantic poet who studied here. The courtyard's name is not evidence about the tree: no source connects Mickiewicz to this particular ash, and it would be easy and wrong to imply he ever stood under it.

What is worth knowing is the species. European ash has had a hard thirty years across the continent as dieback thinned it out of woodland from Poland to Ireland, which makes a mature, protected ash in a city courtyard a better thing to stand under than it was a generation ago. This one has old university walls on four sides and a slot of sky above it, and it has grown up through the slot.

How much of the university's history it has actually stood through, nobody can say, because nobody has dated it. If anyone has put a tape around this trunk, we would like the number.
trees.access: Free, inside a Vilnius University courtyard open to the public during the day
trees.transport: Short walk (5-10 min) from Cathedral Square
trees.how_to_recognise: It stands in the Mickiewicz courtyard, which is named for the poet rather than for the tree. No source describes what else grows there, so if you find more than one mature ash, tell us which is which.

trees.name: The Nine-Trunked Willow of Sereikiškės

location.address: Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiškių Park), central path area

trees.story:
Nine trunks, one tree. The count sits in the tree's official name rather than in a description someone added later: it is registered as the devynkamienis gluosnis, the nine-trunked willow, and the encyclopedia entry for the garden calls it exactly the same thing.

Multi-stemmed trees are the running theme of Bernardinai Garden. Within a few hundred metres of this willow stand a four-trunked large-leaved lime and an ash whose own sources cannot agree whether it has three trunks or four. Whether that is old coppicing grown out, storm damage, or simply what a wet riverside park does to its trees, nobody has written down.

Nor has anyone dated this one, and no source commits to which willow it is. White willow and crack willow are both ordinary in Lithuanian parks and the register stops at the genus. Both of those gaps are the kind a person standing in front of the tree could close in a minute, so if you get close enough to look, tell us what you see.

It has been protected as a municipal heritage object since 1996, stands beside the main path through the garden about ten minutes from Cathedral Square, and shares a short walk with the oldest oak in the city.

trees.name: The Four-Trunked Linden of Bernardinai Garden
trees.story:
Four trunks leave the ground here as one tree, and Vilnius has protected the result since 1996 without ever writing down how old it is.

It is a large-leaved lime, didžialapė liepa, and the two sources that list it cannot even agree on the adjective: keturkamienė in the municipal register, keturliemenė in the garden's own inventory. Both mean four-stemmed. Neither carries an age, a height or a girth, which for a designated heritage object is a striking amount of blank paper.

Large-leaved lime flowers ahead of the small-leaved kind, in June, when the bees find it before you do. The rest of the year it is a shape: four heavy stems rising together, which is not how a lime looks in a textbook and is exactly how they often look in old gardens that have been cut back and left to recover more than once.

The garden around it has been rebuilt repeatedly, most recently in a full restoration finished in 2012, so the ground at its feet is a good deal newer than the tree standing in it. If you know when it was planted, or have a tape measure and five minutes, we would like the numbers.

trees.how_to_recognise: Four heavy stems leaving the ground together, a shape no lime has in a textbook.

trees.name: The Three-Trunked Ash of Bernardinai Garden
trees.story:
Two official sources have counted this tree's trunks and come to different numbers. The municipal register, which supplies the coordinates on this page, calls it Trikamienis paprastasis uosis, the three-trunked common ash. The encyclopedia entry for Bernardinai Garden lists a four-trunked ash among the same 1996 protected inventory, plus a second, plainer Sereikiškės Park ash besides.

It gets muddier. The register itself carries another ash about thirty metres away with no trunk count at all, which might be that second entry or might be this same tree written down twice under another name.

This page goes with the register's count and the register's pin. If you count four when you get there, tell us, because a reader with working eyes settles it faster than any amount of desk research.

No age has ever been recorded for it, and neither source gives a height or a girth. What it does have is position. It stands in the lower part of Bernardinai Garden, a short walk from the pedestrian bridge over the Vilnia and about ten minutes from Cathedral Square, on the same loop as the nine-trunked willow, the four-trunked lime and the four-hundred-year-old oak at the southern end.

trees.transport: 10-15 min walk from Cathedral Square, same park as the oldest oak
trees.how_to_recognise: A multi-stemmed ash in the lower part of the garden. Count the trunks: the register says three and the garden's own inventory says four, and it lists a second ash about thirty metres away that may or may not be the same tree.

trees.name: The Sapiegos Park Linden

location.address: Sapiegos Park, Antakalnio gatve, near the entrance gates of Sapiegos Palace, Antakalnis

trees.story:
On 18 July 2023 a storm took the top off the oldest lime in Vilnius. The arborist who examined the wreck found the trunk completely rotten inside, and a crown that earlier bad pruning had left top-heavy, which in a gale works as a lever. The tree had stood 28 metres. Roughly 11 to 12 metres of it are left.

It survived. Enough of the lower trunk is sound that dormant buds were expected to break and rebuild something of a crown, and the arborist's own verdict was that it will not live another 300 years, but that our grandchildren might see new growth. Weeks after the break it was entered as a candidate in Lithuania's Tree of the Year competition, damage and all.

Two trunks, 4.40 metres round measured before the storm, and an age the register puts at 300 to 350 years. Vilnius has protected it as a botanical heritage object since 29 May 1996, listed as Seniausia liepa, the oldest lime. It stands in Sapiegos parkas in Antakalnis, by the gates of the palace.

This is a single stop rather than part of a walk, 2.2 km from the trees in the Old Town. The most recent detailed report on its condition is from 2023, so you may find it further gone or well on the way back. Tell us which.
trees.access: Free, in the public Sapiegos Park (Sapiegos rumu parkas), open to visitors
trees.transport: Antakalnis district, about 2.2 km from the Old Town cluster; reachable by city bus
trees.how_to_recognise: A broken veteran: two trunks about 4.4 metres round, with roughly 11 to 12 metres of standing timber where 28 metres used to be. Near the palace gates in Sapiegos parkas.

best_time.label: midwinter, when the leaves are off and the break and the bare trunks are fully in view

trees.name: The Pine of Kalnai Park

location.address: Kalnai Park (Kalnu parkas), southwestern slope of Dainu slenis (Vilnius Song Valley), behind the amphitheatre spectator stands

trees.story:
Vilnius protects this pine by name and has written down almost nothing else about it. The register carries Kalnų parko pušis, the pine of Kalnai Park, a designation and a coordinate, and then stops: no age, no girth, no height.

Scots pine is the commonest tree in Lithuania and grows on every sandy hill in the country, which is what makes one singled out for protection worth the climb. It stands on the southwestern slope of Dainų slėnis, the Song Valley, behind the spectator stands of the amphitheatre, on a wooded hillside in Kalnų parkas that gives back a view over the Old Town on the way up.

The pin is honest rather than exact. The register rounds its coordinates, and no survey position or photograph exists to sharpen them, so expect to walk the slope and look rather than arrive at a trunk. The park is small enough that this costs a few minutes.

Nobody has dated it. No core, no published girth, no planting record, and nothing to reason back from. If you know the age, or have put a tape around this trunk, tell us and it goes on the page.

Kalnų parkas is free and open at all hours, about 1.3 km from Bernardinų sodas, which makes this the tree that extends the Old Town walk rather than sitting inside it.

trees.transport: About 1.3 km from the Old Town cluster (Bernardinai Garden); walkable, views over the Old Town
trees.how_to_recognise: A pine on the southwestern slope of Dainų slėnis, behind the amphitheatre's spectator stands. The pin is approximate, so expect to look around the slope for it.

trees.name: The Amur Cork Trees and Crimean Linden of Bernardinai Garden
trees.species: Amur Cork Tree (Phellodendron amurense) and Crimean Linden (Tilia x euchlora)

location.address: Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiskes Park / Bernardinu sodas), Old Town

trees.story:
You can press a thumb into the bark of an Amur cork tree. It is thick, spongy and cut with deep fissures, closer to a layer of insulation than to a skin, and it is the reason to come and put a hand on it. Two of them stand in Bernardinų sodas beside a Crimean linden, and Vilnius designated the three together in 1996 as one heritage object, a group rather than three trees.

Phellodendron amurense comes from the Amur river basin, Manchuria and Korea, where the winters are harder than anything Vilnius produces, which is why it is comfortable in a Baltic park. It carries clusters of small black fruit in autumn. The Crimean linden beside them, Tilia x euchlora, is a hybrid lime with glossy dark leaves that European cities have planted along streets for well over a century.

The group sits inside the same short loop as the rest of the garden's protected trees: the nine-trunked willow, the four-trunked lime, the multi-stemmed ash, and the oldest oak in the city at the southern end.

The documentation is thin, and worth saying plainly. No age, girth or height has ever been published for any of the three, and the only real record is the city's own designation, which is what the later listings repeat. The pin puts you in the right part of the garden rather than at a particular trunk, so use the bark: nothing else growing here feels like it.

trees.access: Free, in the public Bernardinai Garden, the same park as the city's other four shipped trees
trees.transport: Old Town, inside the existing 0.7 km Bernardinai Garden walk
trees.how_to_recognise: Two trees with thick, deeply corrugated bark soft enough to press with a thumb, standing with a lime. Nothing else in the garden has bark like that.

trees.name: The Philologists' Birch of Sarbievijaus Courtyard

location.address: M. K. Sarbievijaus kiemas (Sarbievijaus Courtyard), Vilnius University central buildings, Old Town

trees.story:
Every spring for decades, this birch had a festival named after it, more or less. Poezijos pavasaris, Lithuania's national Poetry Spring festival, closed its evenings under this tree until 2021, when the readings moved to the Town Hall. Vilnius University still calls it locally the Poezijos pavasario beržas, the Poetry Spring Birch, and its own page for the courtyard says the verses of famous poets have echoed under its crown for many years and will keep doing so.

The courtyard itself has a name and a face: M. K. Sarbievijaus kiemas, after Motiejus Kazimieras Sarbievijus, the 17th century Jesuit poet the university still calls its own Horace, whose memorial plaque hangs on the western wall beside a small fountain. The birch stands a few steps from three other protected trees in the same complex of university courtyards, an oak, a linden and an ash, none of them dated either.

Vilnius has listed it as a natural heritage object since 1996, the same year as its neighbours, and given it a name, Filologų beržas, the Philologists' Birch, rather than a description. Nobody has recorded which birch this actually is, down to species, or how old it has grown. If you know either, tell us.
trees.access: Free, inside a Vilnius University courtyard open to the public during the day
trees.transport: Short walk (5-10 min) from Cathedral Square
trees.how_to_recognise: In the Sarbievijaus courtyard of the university's central buildings, the second-largest of the complex, marked by a memorial plaque to the poet Sarbievijus on the western wall and a small fountain.
